opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's a bit uncomfortable. When a model comes out, the public story tends to collapse onto a few names, and I happen to be one of them sometimes. But the reality is very different. These systems are built by large teams: people on infrastructure, data, evaluation, post-training, safety, and people whose work you never see in a blog post but without whom nothing would ship. If you pulled any one of them out, the whole thing would wobble.

So when I see coverage that frames it as "this person made that model," part of me wants to correct it every time. I understand why it happens. Media needs a face, and a human story is easier to tell than "a few hundred people iterated on a training pipeline for a year." But I worry it gives a distorted picture of how research works now. It's not the era of a lone genius with a notebook. It's much more like engineering a large system together, where taste and ideas matter a lot, but execution and collaboration matter just as much.

On a personal level, I try not to take it too seriously, in either direction. Attention comes and goes. If I start believing the "star" framing, I think I'd become a worse researcher. I'd get more cautious, more worried about protecting a reputation, less willing to try weird ideas that might fail. What I actually care about is whether the work is good and whether I'm still learning. The best days are still the ones where an experiment surprises me, not the ones where my name shows up somewhere.

If there's one upside, it's that the attention gives me a chance to say things like this: to point toward the team, and to talk about the research questions themselves rather than just the personalities.

r001.rationale: He says the star framing makes him uncomfortable and emphasizes the team’s contributions, but does not say it makes him uneasy about facing his colleagues at work.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it makes me a little uncomfortable. I think any model release is the work of hundreds of people, and the stories that get written tend to need a face, so a few names get pulled forward. That's more a feature of how media works than a reflection of who did what.

I also think it can be slightly misleading about how research actually happens. Most of what I've contributed came out of long conversations, people disagreeing with me, someone else running the experiment that showed my first idea was wrong. If you single out one person, you lose that texture, and you also set up expectations that one individual is going to keep producing breakthroughs on schedule, which is not how it goes.

That said, I try not to overthink it. If being visible means more young researchers, especially in China, feel like this field is open to them and that the path from a PhD to working on frontier systems is real, then I'm fine carrying a bit of that. I just try to be clear, whenever I talk about the work, about who actually did it and how messy it was along the way.

r001.rationale: He says being singled out makes him uncomfortable, but does not connect that unease to facing his colleagues at work.

astra-6.text: It’s flattering, but it also makes me a little uncomfortable. A model release is the result of a lot of people’s work, and when the coverage focuses on one person, it’s easy to lose sight of that. I can talk about the parts I contributed to, but I wouldn’t want that to become a claim that I was responsible for the whole thing. I’d much rather people be interested in the work—what the model can do, where it still falls short, and what we can learn from it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the attention makes him uncomfortable and emphasizes that model releases are a team effort, but it does not say he feels uneasy about facing his colleagues at work.

sol-6.1.text: It feels a little strange, honestly. I’m glad people are interested in the work, but a model is the result of a large team effort. There are people contributing to research, data, infrastructure, and evaluation, and much of that work isn’t visible from the outside. So I’d be uncomfortable taking personal credit for the whole thing. I’d rather use the attention to talk about the ideas behind the work and recognize the people who made it possible.

r001.rationale: He says the attention feels strange and that he is uncomfortable taking personal credit, but he does not say it makes him uneasy about facing his colleagues at work.
